findings.title: Substring check lets attacker-owned hosts spoof the localhost trustworthy-origin check
findings.explanation: isOriginPotentiallyTrustworthy() is supposed to treat only 127.0.0.0/8, ::1, 'localhost', and names ending in '.localhost' as 'potentially trustworthy' (i.e. as safe as a secure/local origin) per the Fetch/Referrer-Policy and Secure Contexts specs. Instead of anchoring the match, it uses `hostname.includes('localhost.')`, which matches the substring 'localhost.' anywhere in the hostname. Any attacker-registered domain such as `localhost.attacker.com` or `evil-localhost.example.net` satisfies this check even though it is a normal, remote, non-local, plain-HTTP-reachable host fully controlled by the attacker. This function is used by determineRequestsReferrer() (lib/web/fetch/util.js, used from lib/web/fetch/index.js around line 550) to decide whether the Referer header must be downgraded to 'no-referrer'/origin-only when navigating from a trustworthy (https) page to an untrusted destination under the default 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin', 'strict-origin' and 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' policies. Because the attacker's host is misclassified as trustworthy, the downgrade protection is skipped and the referring page's origin (and, depending on policy, more) is sent in the Referer header to the attacker-controlled server, leaking information about what internal/sensitive site the victim was fetching from to a host the user never intended to trust.

findings.title: Predictable Math.random() multipart boundary with unescaped field values enables form-data injection
findings.explanation:
When a FormData body is extracted, the multipart boundary is derived purely from `Math.random()` (`Math.floor(Math.random() * 1e11)`), a non-cryptographic PRNG with a small (~1e11, ~36.5-bit) output space and a recoverable internal state. String field values are only passed through normalizeLinefeeds() (which canonicalizes bare 
/ to 
 but does not remove or escape them) before being embedded verbatim between the part headers and the next boundary; only the field *name* is escaped for CR/LF/quote. If an application forwards attacker-supplied text as a FormData value in an outgoing request (a very common pattern, e.g. proxying a user comment or file field to a backend API), an attacker who can guess or recover the boundary (helped by its low entropy and non-cryptographic generation) can place a literal `
--<boundary>
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="..."` sequence inside their value. Because the value is emitted unescaped, this breaks the parser-side part boundary and injects an entirely new multipart field (e.g. overwriting or adding a privileged field) into the request body that the application did not intend to send.
